meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The road to the Olympics, leads to no city, no country. It goes far beyond New York or Moscow, ancient Greece or Nazi Germany. The road to the Olympics leads — in the end — to the best within us'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Jesse Owens, from his 1980 argument against boycotting Moscow — but the real wording says "Lake Placid," not "New York," and starts a sentence earlier.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1913–1980 · American sprinter and long jumper · four golds at the Berlin Olympics, 1936
answer.sourceLine: Owens really did write this — in the last months of his life, in a bylined article arguing against the American boycott of the 1980 Moscow Olympics, syndicated by the Independent News Alliance and reprinted in full in the Congressional Record of 1 April 1980 ↗. But the wording that circulates has been altered: the article reads “far beyond Lake Placid or Moscow,” and it opens with a sentence the web copies drop, “The road to the Olympics does not lead to Moscow.”

source.excerpt: The road to the Olympics does not lead to Moscow. It leads to no city, no country. It goes far beyond Lake Placid or Moscow, Ancient Greece or Nazi Germany. The road to the Olympics leads, in the end, to the best within us.
trail: January–March 1980 — President Carter demands that American athletes stay away from Moscow. Owens, in the last months of a life that ended on 31 March 1980, tries unsuccessfully to talk him out of it ↗, arguing that the Olympic ideal is meant to be a time-out from war and above politics.

13–24 February 1980 — the Winter Games run in Lake Placid, New York ↗ while the summer boycott is still being fought over. That is the pairing Owens named: the American Games going ahead, and the Soviet Games that might not.

1 April 1980 — the day after Owens dies, Senator Ted Stevens has the article read into the Congressional Record ↗, introducing it as “a story which was published by the Independent News Alliance this year” and printing it entire under the heading “Story by Jesse Owens.” It closes on the four sentences, “far beyond Lake Placid or Moscow.” That reprint, six pages of Owens in the first person, is the earliest located text.

1986, 2001, then 2002 — William J. Baker’s Jesse Owens: An American Life (New York: Free Press) ↗ becomes the citation later writers point back to, and Smith’s Black Heroes still prints “Lake Placid or Moscow” ↗. Then a Voice of America Special English profile written by Barbara Dash ↗ renders it “New York or Moscow” and drops the opening sentence — and that is the version the quote databases copied.
source.excerptNote: This is the wording of Owens’s own article as the Congressional Record printed it on 1 April 1980 ↗, and the same four sentences run through the later print record — the Record again in 1991, a 1997 public-speaking textbook, and Jessie Carney Smith’s Black Heroes (2001) ↗. Later printings contract the opening to “doesn’t” and lower-case “ancient Greece.” The version that circulates online drops that opening sentence altogether and replaces Lake Placid with New York.

source.rightsNote: The article was published in 1980, and anything first published in the United States in 1931 or later is presumed still in copyright, so this line should be treated as in copyright rather than free to reproduce. The 1980 syndicating publisher is named in the Congressional Record as the Independent News Alliance; how the copyright is now divided between Owens’s estate and whoever succeeded that syndicate has not been traced, so both are named here as the conservative default. Short quotation with attribution is normal practice, but wholesale reuse is not something this page can clear.

author.name: Jesse Owens
author.heading: Who was Jesse Owens?
author.metaLine: 1913–1980 · American sprinter and long jumper · four gold medals at Berlin 1936
author.bio: James Cleveland “Jesse” Owens was born in Oakville, Alabama, in 1913 and won four gold medals at the 1936 Berlin Olympics — the 100 metres, the 200 metres, the long jump and the 4×100-metre relay — in front of Hitler. Fame did not translate into a living: he returned to a segregated America, raced against horses for money, went bankrupt, and only much later became a paid goodwill ambassador and public speaker, receiving the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1976. He spent the final months of his life arguing, unsuccessfully, that President Carter should drop his demand that the United States boycott the Moscow Games; he died of lung cancer in Tucson, Arizona, on 31 March 1980.

Also quoted in William J. Baker, Jesse Owens: An American Life (New York: Free Press, 1986), and reprinted in Jessie Carney Smith, Black Heroes (Visible Ink Press, 2001). misattribution.heading: What the internet gets wrong
misattribution.intro: The name on this one is right. The words are not — and the two changes between what Owens said in 1980 and what the quote sites print are precisely the two that empty it of its argument.

items.why: Owens’s own article carries “far beyond Lake Placid or Moscow,” as the Congressional Record printed it on 1 April 1980 ↗; the same wording runs on through the Record of 1991, a 1997 public-speaking textbook, and Jessie Carney Smith’s Black Heroes (2001) ↗. Lake Placid is a village in New York State, and it hosted the Winter Games from 13 to 24 February 1980 ↗. Owens was naming the two 1980 Olympics against each other — the American one going ahead, the Soviet one under threat. Enlarging the town into the state leaves “New York,” which was hosting nothing.

Owens began: “The road to the Olympics does not lead to Moscow.” That is the claim; the famous sentences are its supporting argument. Cut it, and what is left starts at “leads to no city, no country” and reads as motivational wallpaper rather than a specific, unpopular position taken in a live political fight.

Wikiquote files the line under ‘decade unknown’ and cites a Voice of America programme broadcast on 7 June 2002 ↗ — a radio profile made long after Owens’s death, which itself gives no date or occasion. That citation is why almost every quote page presents this as a timeless Olympic aphorism instead of a dated intervention in the boycott of 1980.

misattribution.truthLine: Owens wrote it in 1980, and he wrote it to argue that Americans should go to Moscow. The version that travels has had the boycott taken out of it — but the argument survives whole, in his own words, in the Congressional Record of 1 April 1980 ↗, the day after he died. Quote Investigator has traced two other Owens lines, but not this one ↗.

context.heading: Why he said it
lead: In January 1980 President Jimmy Carter told the United States Olympic Committee that American athletes would not go to Moscow that summer unless Soviet troops left Afghanistan. Jesse Owens — the one American whose Olympic record was itself a political argument — came down against the boycott. He had spent forty years being invoked as the man who beat Hitler at Hitler’s own Games, and his conclusion from that was the opposite of the one Washington was drawing: you win these arguments by turning up, not by staying home.

That is the sentence the internet has lost. Owens did not open with uplift. He opened with a refusal: the road to the Olympics does not lead to Moscow — meaning the Games are not the property of the country hosting them, so a host country’s crimes are not a reason to abandon them. Everything after that is the proof: not Lake Placid, where the Winter Games were running that February; not Moscow; not ancient Greece; not Berlin in 1936, which he knew better than anyone. He did not live to see the vote. He died on 31 March 1980.
detailsBody: The form is settled: Owens wrote it. The Congressional Record of 1 April 1980 introduces the passage as coming from “a story which was published by the Independent News Alliance this year” and prints the whole thing under the heading “Story by Jesse Owens,” in the first person — a syndicated newspaper article, not an off-the-cuff answer. That squares with a July 1984 magazine notice, found only as a search snippet, which says Owens “wrote” the words “in a March 1980 article strongly opposing the U.S. boycott of Moscow’s Games.” Jessie Carney Smith’s Black Heroes later frames him as “responding to reporters’ questions regarding the upcoming Olympics” — a secondary description written two decades on, and the odd one out.

What is still open is narrower: which newspapers ran the Independent News Alliance release, and on what date. The text itself is stable. Searches of digitised print return the same four sentences from 1980 onward — in the Congressional Record for 1980 and again in 1991, in a 1997 public-speaking textbook, and in Black Heroes in 2001 — always with “Lake Placid or Moscow,” always with the opening line intact. The trimmed, re-lettered version appears in a Voice of America radio profile, and from there in the quote databases.

He wrote it in an article opposing the 1980 Moscow boycott, syndicated by the Independent News Alliance and reprinted in full in the Congressional Record of 1 April 1980. sourcesVerified.claim: The Congressional Record, Senate, 1 April 1980 (96th Cong., 2d sess., vol. 126 pt. 6, pp. 7247-48) records Senator Ted Stevens saying "Mr. President, Jesse Owens wrote a story which was published by the Independent News Alliance this year. In that story he points out his position with regard to the 1980 summer games", and then, on unanimous consent, prints the piece in full under the heading "STORY BY JESSE OWENS". It closes: "The road to the Olympics does not lead to Moscow. It leads to no city, no country. It goes far beyond Lake Placid or Moscow, Ancient Greece or Nazi Germany. The road to the Olympics leads, in the end, to the best within us." (The unanimous-consent line renders the syndicate as "Independence News Alliance", evidently a slip or OCR artefact for the same name.)
Wikiquote lists this line under "decade unknown" with the wording "It goes far beyond New York or Moscow", citing: As quoted in People In America: "Jesse Owens" by Barbara Dash on VOA (7 June 2002).

Jesse Owens was born 12 September 1913 in Oakville, Alabama and died 31 March 1980 in Tucson, Arizona; he won four gold medals at the 1936 Berlin Olympics; he received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1976; and "A few months before his death, Owens had unsuccessfully tried to convince President Jimmy Carter to withdraw his demand that the United States boycott the 1980 Moscow Olympics ... He argued that the Olympic ideal was supposed to be observed as a time-out from war and that it was above politics."
The 1980 Winter Olympics were held from 13 to 24 February 1980 in Lake Placid, New York, United States.
In January 1980 President Carter announced that the United States would not participate in the Moscow Olympics unless Soviet forces withdrew from Afghanistan.

The Voice of America Special English profile of Jesse Owens, written by Barbara Dash, contains: 'The road to the Olympics,' he said, 'leads to no city, no country. It goes far beyond New York or Moscow, ancient Greece or Nazi Germany. The road to the Olympics leads -- in the end -- to the best within us.' The programme gives no date or occasion for the statement. NOTE: this transcript is headed "Jesse Owens, 1913-1980: He Was Once the World's Fastest Runner" and dated VOA Special English 2008-12-20 (produced by Lawan Davis) — it is a later rebroadcast of the Dash script, not the 7 June 2002 broadcast Wikiquote cites, and it carries no 2002 date itself.
Jessie Carney Smith's Black Heroes (Visible Ink Press, 2001) contains a page matching the exact phrase "Lake Placid or Moscow" — the wording the online version replaces with "New York".
William J. Baker's Jesse Owens: An American Life is a 1986 biography published by Free Press, New York (and Collier Macmillan, London); the Internet Archive copy is access-restricted.
Quote Investigator's Jesse Owens tag page lists only two articles — both about "find the good" — and none investigating "the road to the Olympics" or "the best within us".

A Google Books full-text search for the phrase "ancient Greece or Nazi Germany" returns the Congressional Record vol. 126 (1980), the Congressional Record (1991), Osborn & Osborn's Public Speaking (1997) and Smith's Black Heroes (2001), each with the reading "Lake Placid or Moscow"; the 1997 textbook snippet also shows the opening sentence "The road to the Olympics does not lead to Moscow."

Michael and Suzanne Osborn's Public Speaking (Houghton Mifflin, 1997) is a real 513-page third-edition textbook — the volume whose snippet carries the fuller Owens wording. Note: Google Books' in-volume search returned no match for the phrase when fetched directly, so only the bibliographic details are treated as confirmed from this page.
